In [[probability]] and [[statistics]], the '''reciprocal distribution''', also known as the '''log-uniform distribution''', is a [[continuous probability distribution]]. It is characterised by its [[probability density function]], within the support of the distribution, being proportional to the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of the variable.

The reciprocal distribution is an example of an [[inverse distribution]], and the reciprocal (inverse) of a random variable with a reciprocal distribution itself has a reciprocal distribution.

==Definition==

The [[probability density function]] (pdf) of the reciprocal distribution is

: <math> f( x; a,b ) = \frac{ 1 }{ x [ \ln( b ) - \ln( a ) ]} \quad  \text{ for } a \le x \le b \text{ and } a > 0.</math>

Here, <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are the parameters of the distribution, which are the lower and upper bounds of the [[Support of a distribution|support]], and <math>\ln</math> is the [[natural log]]. The [[cumulative distribution function]] is

: <math> F( x ; a,b) = \frac{ \ln( x ) - \ln( a ) }{ \ln( b ) - \ln( a ) } \quad  \text{ for } a \le x \le b.</math>

== Characterization ==

=== Relationship between the log-uniform and the uniform distribution ===

[[File:Reciprocal Histogram.svg|thumb|left|Histogram and log-histogram of random deviates from the reciprocal distribution]]

A positive random variable ''X'' is log-uniformly distributed if the logarithm of ''X'' is uniform distributed,

:<math> \ln(X) \sim \mathcal U(\ln(a), \ln(b)).</math>

This relationship is true regardless of the base of the logarithmic or exponential function. If <math>\log_a(Y)</math> is uniform distributed, then so is <math>\log_b(Y)</math>, for any two positive numbers <math>a,b\neq 1</math>. Likewise, if <math>e^X</math> is log-uniform distributed, then so is <math>a^X</math>, where <math>0 < a \neq 1</math>.

==Applications==

The reciprocal distribution is of considerable importance in [[numerical analysis]], because a [[computer]]’s arithmetic operations, in particular, repeated multiplications and/or divisions, transform [[Significand|mantissa]]s with initial arbitrary distributions into the reciprocal distribution as a limiting distribution.<ref name=Hamming1970>[[Richard Hamming|Hamming R. W.]] (1970) [https://archive.org/details/bstj49-8-1609 "On the distribution of numbers"], ''The Bell System Technical Journal'' 49(8) 1609–1625</ref>
